dossier.purpose: Python library and `trafilatura` command-line tool that fetches web pages over plain HTTP(S) (urllib3, optional pycurl) or reads local HTML/stdin, extracts main text, comments and metadata (title, author, date, site name, URL, tags, categories, license) with a rule-based extractor backed by readability/jusText fallbacks, and emits TXT, Markdown, CSV, JSON, HTML, XML or XML-TEI. It also discovers URLs through feeds, sitemaps and a small focused crawler. It does not run JavaScript or drive a browser. Every statement in this dossier comes from static reading of the files at the pinned commit (commit confirmed via .git/HEAD:1 and .git/packed-refs:2); nothing was executed, installed or benchmarked.

claims.claim: Trafilatura is a Python package and command-line tool designed to gather text on the Web and simplify the process of turning raw HTML into structured, meaningful data.
It includes all necessary discovery and text processing components to perform web crawling, downloads, scraping, and extraction of main texts, metadata and comments.
It aims at staying handy and modular: no database is required, the output can be converted to commonly used formats.
Support for sitemaps (TXT, XML) and feeds (ATOM, JSON, RSS); smart crawling and URL management (filtering and deduplication).
Parallel processing of online and offline input: live URLs, efficient and polite processing of download queues; previously downloaded HTML files and parsed HTML trees.
Main text (common patterns and generic algorithms like jusText and readability); metadata (title, author, date, site name, categories and tags); optional comments, links, images, tables.
Output formats: TXT and Markdown, CSV, JSON, HTML, XML and XML-TEI.
Optional add-ons: language detection on extracted content; speed optimizations.
Actively maintained with support from the open-source community; 'this package continues to be maintained but its future depends on community support'.
'Trafilatura consistently outperforms other open-source libraries in text extraction benchmarks'; benchmark section and evaluation readme are linked.

Other evaluations: 'Most efficient open-source library' in ScrapingHub's article extraction benchmark; 'Best overall tool' (Lejeune & Barbaresi 2020); 'Best single tool by ROUGE-LSum Mean F1 Page Scores' (Bevendorff et al. 2023).
Usage documentation is provided for the command line, Python and R (install command is not in the README itself, it links to the docs).
Distributed under the Apache 2.0 license; versions prior to v1.8.0 are under GPLv3+.

No account, API key or hosted service is needed for the CLI/library (searched for key/token/credential: none). TEI validation uses the bundled DTD, no download (xml.py:34, 288-290). The Sphinx docs-site config embeds a Google Analytics ID with IP anonymization (docs/conf.py:99-102): website only, not the package. Network behaviour inside dependencies (courlan, htmldate, justext) is outside this repo; only courlan's redirection_test HEAD helper is visibly called (downloads.py:23, 349-356).

code.architecture: One pure-Python package `trafilatura/` (21 modules, ~8.9k lines) plus settings.cfg and a bundled TEI DTD (trafilatura/data/tei_corpus.dtd). Flow: cli.py (argparse) -> cli_utils.py (input loading, courlan UrlStore throttled download queue, file/stdin pipelines, output writing) -> downloads.py (urllib3 pool, or pycurl when installed; Response class) -> core.py (extract / bare_extraction / extract_with_metadata). The cascade in core.trafilatura_sequence (core.py:179-287): main_extractor.py rule-based extraction using xpaths.py -> external.py comparison with readability (in-tree fork readability_lxml.py) and jusText -> baseline.py rescue -> recall-mode retry. Supporting modules: utils.py (decompression, encoding detection, load_html), htmlprocessing.py (tree cleaning/conversion), metadata.py + json_metadata.py (OpenGraph/meta/JSON-LD; dates via htmldate), deduplication.py (LRU cache, Simhash fingerprint), xml.py (TXT/Markdown/CSV/JSON/XML/TEI serialization and TEI validation), settings.py (Extractor/Document, constants), feeds.py / sitemaps.py / spider.py (URL discovery, spider.py holds the robots.txt logic), meta.py (cache reset). No browser engine, no server, no database, no persistent state except files written with -o/--backup-dir.
code.packaging_and_release: setuptools build backend (pyproject.toml:2-4); single package `trafilatura` (pyproject.toml:67-68); version read from trafilatura/__init__.py:10 (pyproject.toml:71-72); package data = settings.cfg + TEI DTD (pyproject.toml:75-79); ships py.typed (MANIFEST.in:4). Pure Python: no compiled extensions in this repo. MANIFEST.in controls the sdist (excludes tests/realworld_tests.py and tests/cache, lines 9-10; line 1 still names README.rst although the README is Markdown, pyproject.toml:9). Distribution channel is PyPI (docs/installation.rst:35) plus a Homebrew formula mentioned in the docs (docs/installation.rst:65); CITATION.cff:6-9 points to a Zenodo concept DOI for archived releases. The repo has NO release/publish workflow (.github/workflows contains only tests.yml and codeql.yml) and no checksums, signatures or provenance attestations are configured or documented, so how PyPI artifacts are built and uploaded cannot be determined from the repo. Changelog: HISTORY.md (no release dates).
code.tests_and_ci: pytest (pytest>=9.1.1, pytest-cov; pyproject.toml:92-100, 162-163, testpaths `tests/*test*.py`). 13 test modules in tests/ (baseline, cli, deduplication, downloads, feeds, filters, json_metadata, metadata, realworld, sitemaps, spider, unit, xml_tei) with ~235 `def test_` functions, plus tests/conftest.py (mock_network fixture, conftest.py:1-83) and docs/docs_tests.py (Sphinx build with -W). Fixtures: tests/cache (110 pages), tests/eval (926 pages), tests/resources (21 files). Some tests call live hosts (httpbun.com: tests/downloads_tests.py:124-188, tests/cli_tests.py:295-304). CI: .github/workflows/tests.yml on push/PR to master: ubuntu-latest x Python 3.10/3.12/3.14 x MINIMAL true/false, ubuntu 3.13 full, macos-latest 3.11, windows-latest 3.11 (lines 15-34); steps: `uv pip install -e .[dev]`, `ruff check` + `ruff format --check`, libcurl dev + `.[all]` on full jobs, `mypy -p trafilatura` (3.13 full), `pytest --cov`, docs build test, Codecov upload with CODECOV_TOKEN (lines 53-101). .github/workflows/codeql.yml: CodeQL for Python on push/PR to master plus weekly cron. risks: Scope: no JavaScript rendering, browser automation, form/POST, sign-in, tab, screenshot or PDF handling exists in the package. Downloads are plain HTTP GET via urllib3 or pycurl (trafilatura/downloads.py:209-215, 437-512) with no Content-Type handling (downloads.py:241-250); only a static Cookie/User-Agent can come from settings.cfg (settings.cfg:13-19). The docs send JS-heavy pages to external browser-automation libraries such as Playwright (docs/troubleshooting.rst:35-39). Extraction can take HTML from stdin or --input-dir (cli.py:218-229), so it can only sit downstream of such a tool.

Attribution output is thin and partly implicit: JSON `source` is the page-declared og:url/canonical when present, with the requested URL only a fallback (metadata.py:190-197, 372-396, 515-517; cli_utils.py:263). The CLI discards the final redirect URL, HTTP status and headers (fetch_url returns text only, downloads.py:263-288; the full Response is available only through Python fetch_response, :291-319) and emits no fetch timestamp: `filedate` is a date-only value, present in JSON only (metadata.py:560; settings.py:216-222; xml.py:159-180). HTML piped on stdin or read with --input-dir cannot be given an origin URL on the CLI (cli.py:222-229). Metadata appears only with --with-metadata (settings.py:168-170). JSON/CSV field sets are defined only in code (xml.py:159-180, 637-653), not documented, and lightly tested (tests/unit_tests.py:293-296).

TLS verification is silently downgraded: on an SSL error both HTTP paths retry with certificate verification disabled (downloads.py:232-234 urllib3; 459-463 and 485-487 pycurl), urllib3's InsecureRequestWarning is globally silenced (downloads.py:58), and the HEAD liveness probe never verifies (downloads.py:330-332). Tests assert the fallback (tests/downloads_tests.py:202-228). Only a log line marks it; there is no option to disable the fallback (a --no-ssl flag exists only as commented-out code, cli.py:110-112). Relevant where attribution depends on an authenticated origin.

robots.txt compliance is limited to the crawler's link filter, which uses the generic '*' agent (spider.py:86-88, 150-168). Direct downloads (-u, -i, --feed, --sitemap) do not check it (no robots logic in downloads.py or cli_utils.py). The default User-Agent identifies the tool (downloads.py:81-82); docs warn it may be blocked and that downloads do not bypass blocks (docs/troubleshooting.rst:56, 67-68).

Failure semantics for shell callers (static reading, not executed): exit status reflects only download failures, 0/1/126 (cli_utils.py:260-267, 382-391). An extraction that returns None (empty, too short, language-filtered) prints nothing to stdout and still exits 0 (cli_utils.py:443-465; stdin path cli.py:226-229). There is no output-length cap option (cli.py:49-152; settings.cfg). URL-mode extraction has no time limit (cli_utils.py:443-465); EXTRACTION_TIMEOUT is used only by the --input-dir pipeline via executor.map(..., timeout=...) whose result iterator is never consumed (cli_utils.py:428-437), so by code reading it cannot fire; docs describe it as dropping extraction after 30 s and mention the `signal` module, which the code does not use (docs/settings.rst:39).

Python-API state and resource caveats: the urllib3 pool and retry strategy are process-global singletons built from the first config seen (downloads.py:59-61, 166-200), so later per-call DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT/MAX_REDIRECTS changes are ignored on the urllib3 path (tests reset them by hand, tests/downloads_tests.py:71-85, 164-167). Decompression of fetched payloads has no output-size cap (utils.py:116-138, with a `max_output_size=???` note at :124), so MAX_FILE_SIZE bounds only the compressed size where trafilatura itself decompresses (e.g. the pycurl path sets Accept-Encoding by hand and fetches the raw body, downloads.py:78-80, 442-450, 473).

Docs drift from code (code should be trusted): docs/downloads.rst:175, 208, 218-220, 244 import `get_crawl_delay` from trafilatura (not present; only courlan's UrlStore method is used, spider.py:327) and unpack 4 values from load_download_buffer (it returns 2, downloads.py:390-397); docs/index.rst:198 cites a docs/requirements.txt that is not in the repo; docs/usage-r.rst:102 shows XML metadata attributes (`source=`) that the code does not emit by default (xml.py:66-80, 224-229; settings.py:168-170); docs/downloads.rst:134 states exit code 1 on failures while the code also returns 126 (cli_utils.py:382-391). The hosted HTTP API is documented as unavailable and closed-source (docs/usage-api.rst:20-21, 105).

Maintenance and supply chain: one listed author (pyproject.toml:13-15); the README says the future depends on community support (README.md:143-144; CONTRIBUTING.md:4-6). No release/publish workflow, checksums, signatures, attestations, lockfile or security policy in the repo (.github/workflows has only tests.yml and codeql.yml). CI actions are pinned by tag, not commit SHA (tests.yml:38, 42, 47, 95; codeql.yml:28, 32, 46, 59) and tests.yml has no permissions block. Some tests hit live third-party hosts (tests/downloads_tests.py:124-188; tests/cli_tests.py:295-304). The published benchmark table predates 2.x (docs/evaluation.rst:74-78). Three dependencies (courlan, htmldate, py3langid) are the same author's projects.
